lessons.title: Customer needs and market segmentation
objectives: Explain why understanding customer needs is vital for a new business
Describe market segmentation and the main ways of segmenting a market

keywords.def: the things customers require from a product, such as price, quality and choice
where buyers and sellers meet to trade a good or service
dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics
characteristics of a population such as age, gender and income
the group of customers a business aims its product at

starter: Define 'added value'.
What is a USP?
Give one reason why products become obsolete.

teach.heading: What do customers want?
bullets: Price: is it affordable?
Quality: does it last and work?
Choice: are there options?
Convenience: is it easy to buy and use?
teach.note: Make clear these are the customer needs a business must meet. Ask pupils to rank them for a school lunch and then for a laptop to see priorities change. Add that for Muslim customers, halal certification can be an essential need, not an optional extra.

teach.heading: Why identify customers?
bullets: Avoid wasting money on the wrong product
Match the product to customers' needs
Decide price and promotion sensibly
Build loyalty and repeat sales
teach.note: A common error is saying 'everyone is a customer'. Explain that small businesses have limited money, so they must focus. Ask what would happen if a modest-fashion shop advertised to everyone in the country.

teach.heading: Market segmentation
bullets: Split a market into groups
Each group has similar needs
A business can then target the right group
More effective than selling to everyone
teach.note: Define segmentation clearly, then target market. A segment is one part; the target market is the segment(s) chosen.

teach.heading: Ways to segment
bullets: Demographics: age, gender, income, family size
Location: urban, rural, region
Lifestyle: sports fans, busy parents, vegetarians
Income: budget, mid-range, premium
teach.note: Give a worked example: a gym could segment by age (teenagers, adults, over 60s), lifestyle (competitive athletes or relaxers) and location. Ask pupils to produce a segment for a halal ready-meal brand: busy professionals aged 25 to 40 in cities.

teach.heading: Worked example: Zayd's sportswear
bullets: Segment: boys aged 11 to 16 who play football
Need: affordable, hard-wearing kit
Place: online and school team orders
Promotion: social media and local clubs
teach.note: Use this to model a short analysis answer: identify segment, give reason, link to marketing choice. Ask pupils to find a second segment Zayd could add and why.

practice: Name two customer needs a family would consider when choosing a restaurant.
A business sells prayer mats online. Identify two ways it could segment its market.
Explain why a bookshop might target students rather than the whole population.
independent: Choose a product of your own and describe its target market using at least three types of segmentation.
Explain two benefits to a small business of segmenting its market (Explain: a point developed with two linked expansion points).
Write a paragraph assessing whether price or quality is more important to customers of a school uniform supplier.
exit: Define 'market segmentation'.
Give two ways a market can be segmented.
lessons.homework: Look at an advert and write five sentences identifying its target market and the evidence for it.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching cards for segment type and example. Stretch: explain why segments can overlap and how a business decides which one to prioritise.

lessons.title: Revenue, costs and profit
objectives: Calculate revenue, total costs and profit or loss
Distinguish fixed from variable costs and explain how interest affects a business

keywords.def: the money a business receives from selling goods or services (price x quantity)
costs that stay the same however much is produced, such as rent
costs that change with output, such as ingredients
fixed costs plus variable costs
revenue minus total costs; if negative it is a loss

starter: Define a SMART objective.
Give one financial aim and one non-financial aim.
Why is survival important for a new business?

teach.heading: Revenue
bullets: Revenue = price x quantity sold
Also called turnover or sales revenue
Revenue is not profit
Example: 400 bars at 3 pounds = 1,200 pounds
teach.note: Misconception: revenue and profit are the same. Ask: if you sell 400 bars for 3 pounds each and spend 1,300 pounds, did you profit? (No, a loss of 100 pounds.)

teach.heading: Fixed and variable costs
bullets: Fixed: rent, insurance, salaries
Variable: ingredients, packaging
Total costs = fixed + variable
Variable costs rise with output
teach.note: Hold up a cup: its cup and ingredients are variable costs; the café rent is fixed. Ask pupils to classify more examples. Variable cost = variable cost per unit x number of units.

teach.heading: Calculating profit
bullets: Profit = revenue - total costs
Negative profit is a loss
Check units and months match
Show working in exams
teach.note: Present the worked example fully on the board.

teach.heading: Worked example: Yusuf's date-and-oat bars
bullets: Price 3 pounds, 400 bars sold
Revenue = 3 x 400 = 1,200 pounds
Variable cost 1.20 per bar = 480 pounds
Fixed costs 240; total 720; profit 480 pounds
teach.note: Write out each step. Check: 240 + 480 = 720; 1,200 - 720 = 480. Ask: what happens if Yusuf sells only 150 bars? Revenue 450, variable 180, total 420, profit 30. Show that costs do not fall in proportion.

teach.heading: Interest and honest pricing
bullets: Interest is the cost of borrowing money
Higher borrowing raises costs
Muslim entrepreneurs avoid riba (interest)
Halal options: savings, partners, profit-sharing
teach.note: Present as a note, not exam content. Qur'an 2:275 states that Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba. Many Muslim business owners start with savings or partners sharing risk and profit. Also tie to honest pricing: a fair price and accurate weights and measures (Qur'an 83:1-3 warns against cheating in measure).

practice: Calculate revenue: a stall sells 250 scarves at 8 pounds each.
A café has rent of 500 pounds a month and variable costs of 2 pounds per drink. Calculate total costs for 600 drinks.
Using your answers, calculate the profit if the café sells 600 drinks at 3.50 pounds.
independent: A business sells 300 notebooks at 4 pounds. Fixed costs 350 pounds, variable cost 1.50 per notebook. Calculate revenue, total costs and profit.
Explain two reasons why a business might make a loss even if sales are high (Explain: a point developed with two linked expansion points).
Write a paragraph assessing whether a start-up should focus on cutting costs or increasing revenue.
exit: Calculate revenue: 120 items sold at 15 pounds each.
Give one fixed cost and one variable cost for a bakery.
lessons.homework: Create your own business with a price and costs, and calculate its revenue, total costs and profit for one month.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: worked calculation frames with boxes to fill. Stretch: calculate profit if price rises 10 percent and sales fall 5 percent.

lessons.title: 1.1 Business aims and objectives (core)
lessons.bigQuestion: A new home bakery and a global supermarket chain: would they have the same aims? Why or why not?
objectives: To understand how aims and objectives guide a business and why they change as it grows
successCriteria: All: define aim and objective and give two financial aims
Most: classify aims as financial or non-financial in a case
Some: explain why a named trigger changes an objective
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages for market share and SMART targets
lessons.smsc: Moral: halal earning and fair dealing as business aims

keywords.def: the long-term goal of a business
a measurable, timed target that helps reach an aim
a firm's sales as a percentage of total market sales
staying in business

hook.text: A new home bakery and a global supermarket chain: would they have the same aims? Why or why not?
hook.a: No: a start-up often aims to survive; a large firm may aim for market share or growth. Aims change with size and conditions.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'O you who have believed, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly but only in lawful business by mutual consent' (An-Nisa' 4:29). A Muslim's business aims include halal earning and fair dealing, not profit at any cost.

starter.a: something done for you, like a haircut
options: something done for you, like a haircut

starter.q: Name one business near you and one thing it wants to achieve.
starter.a: e.g. a corner shop wants to survive and make a profit.

teach.heading: Aims and objectives
bullets: Aim: the long-term goal
Objective: a measurable step towards it
SMART objectives: specific, measurable, timed
teach.note: Example: aim 'grow'; objective 'increase sales by 10% in 12 months'.

teach.heading: Financial and non-financial aims
teach.note: Spec 1.1.1.

teach.heading: Why objectives change (1.1.2)
teach.note: Use a fictional firm: Noor Bakes, a home bakery that grows into three shops.

misconception.wrong: An aim and an objective are the same thing
misconception.right: An objective is a measurable, timed target that helps reach the aim

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: Which is an objective rather than an aim?
options: Increase market share from 5% to 8% by December
check.why: Only option A is measurable and timed; the others are broad aims.

practice.q: Outline one reason why Noor Bakes might change its objective from survival to growth. (2 marks)
practice.a: It has built a loyal customer base and steady profits (performance), so it can aim to open more shops.
practice.model: Point: performance has improved. Development: Noor Bakes now makes a steady profit and has regular customers, so survival is secure and it can set a growth objective such as opening a second shop.

practice.q: Market share is an example of ...

independent.q: In the portal response box, explain two non-financial aims a social enterprise might have (sentence starter: 'One non-financial aim is ...').
independent.a: e.g. social objectives (training young people); personal satisfaction for the founders; each developed.
independent.model: The teacher writes the first: 'One non-financial aim is a social objective, such as training young people from the area, because the business exists to help the community as well as to cover its costs.'

independent.q: Extend: write a SMART objective for a charity shop.
independent.a: e.g. raise £5,000 for the local food bank by 31 July.

independent.q: Stretch: 'Profit should always be the main aim of a business.' Give one argument for and one against.
independent.a: For: needed to survive and grow. Against: social or ethical aims may matter more; halal earning means profit within limits.

exit.q: Which is a trigger that can change objectives?
exit.a: New legislation

exit.q: Back to our ponder: A new home bakery and a global supermarket chain: would they have the same aims? Why or why not?
exit.a: No: a start-up often aims to survive; a large firm may aim for market share or growth. Aims change with size and conditions.

lessons.send: SEND: key-word card and a partly completed answer frame. EAL: glossary with examples. Stretch: add a counter-argument and a judgement.

lessons.title: 1.2 Business ownership (core): sole traders, partnerships and companies
lessons.bigQuestion: If your business failed and owed £50,000, should the bank be able to take your family car? What would you choose before starting?
objectives: To understand how forms of business ownership differ in risk, liability, control and finance
successCriteria: All: describe a sole trader, partnership, private and public limited company
Most: explain limited and unlimited liability
Some: judge which ownership form suits a given business
lessons.smsc: Moral: sharing risk fairly; partnership in Islamic finance

keywords.def: a business owned and run by one person
a business owned by two or more people who share profit and risk
owners lose only what they invested
an owner of part of a company

hook.text: If your business failed and owed £50,000, should the bank be able to take your family car? What would you choose before starting?
hook.a: With unlimited liability (sole trader, partnership) it could; with a limited company the owners lose only what they invested.

islamicLink.text: Islam encourages partnership in trade: Islamic finance uses mushārakah (مُشَارَكَة), where partners share profit and loss, instead of interest-based loans. Islamic note: riba (رِبَا) is forbidden (Qur'an 2:275: Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba). Islamic finance uses partnership (mushārakah, مُشَارَكَة) and cost-plus sale (murābaḥah, مُرَابَحَة) instead.

starter.q: Name a business with one owner.

teach.heading: Four common forms
teach.note: Spec 1.2.1. Fictional examples only.

head: Form
Owners
Liability
Example
rows: Shareholders, shares not on the stock exchange

teach.heading: Limited and unlimited liability
bullets: Unlimited: personal assets can be taken
Limited: lose only the money invested
Limited liability encourages investment
teach.note: Return to the ponder question.

teach.heading: Other forms (1.2.3)
bullets: Franchise: buy the right to use a brand
Social enterprise: profits reinvested for a social aim
Public corporation: owned by the government
Multinational: operates in more than one country

misconception.wrong: A private limited company is owned by the government
misconception.right: 'Private' means its shares are not sold to the public; public corporations are government-owned

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: Which owners have limited liability?
check.why: Only company shareholders have limited liability; the others are personally liable for debts.

practice.q: Explain one disadvantage of being a sole trader. (3 marks)
practice.a: Unlimited liability: if the business fails, personal assets such as savings or a car may be used to pay debts, so the owner carries all the risk.
practice.model: Point: unlimited liability. Explain: the owner and the business are legally the same. Develop: so if debts cannot be paid, personal possessions can be taken.

independent.q: Case (pupil PDF): Amir and Sara want to open a café. In the portal box, justify whether they should form a partnership or a private limited company (frame: 'I recommend ... because ... However ... Overall ...').
independent.a: Either, if justified: Ltd for limited liability and credibility; partnership for simplicity and privacy; must weigh risk against cost and control.
independent.model: The teacher writes the opening: 'I recommend a private limited company because the café needs about £40,000 of equipment, and limited liability protects their homes if it fails.'

independent.q: Extend: give one advantage and one disadvantage of a franchise.
independent.a: Advantage: known brand. Disadvantage: royalty payments and less control.

independent.q: Stretch: why might a plc lose control to outsiders?
independent.a: Anyone can buy shares; a large shareholder can influence decisions.

exit.q: A social enterprise uses its profits mainly to ...
exit.a: pursue a social aim

exit.q: Back to our ponder: If your business failed and owed £50,000, should the bank be able to take your family car? What would you choose before starting?
exit.a: With unlimited liability (sole trader, partnership) it could; with a limited company the owners lose only what they invested.

lessons.title: Companies and public corporations: limited liability
lessons.bigQuestion: Why would an owner want their house protected from business debts?
objectives: Describe private limited companies, public limited companies and public corporations
Explain limited liability and shares
Compare forms by risk, control, finance and use of profit
successCriteria: All: define limited liability and name three business forms
Most: compare a private and public limited company
Some: explain why a growing business might change its form
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: dividends as a share of profit; percentage ownership
lessons.smsc: Moral: transparency and honest accounts when the public can buy shares

keywords.def: owners can lose only the money they invested
shares sold privately, not to the public; has limited liability
can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange
an owner of a company who holds shares
a share of profit paid to shareholders
a business owned and controlled by the government

starter: Define unlimited liability.
Give two features of a partnership.
Sami and Yusuf's business owes 20,000 pounds. Who is responsible?

teach.heading: Limited liability and shares
bullets: A company is a separate legal person from its owners
Owners (shareholders) can lose only what they invested
Money is raised by selling shares
Profits are paid as dividends
teach.note: Use the fictional Zayn's Solar Ltd. Four shareholders invest 10,000 each. If it owes 100,000 and collapses, each can lose only the 10,000 invested, not house or savings. Contrast with sole trader. Do not teach company accounts; stay at concept level. For Muslim pupils, note that investing in a company by buying shares is discussed by scholars, and the teacher may expand on which businesses and structures are considered permissible; do not give rulings.

teach.heading: Private and public limited companies
teach.note: Compare table. Key facts: Ltd shares are not for sale to the general public and are sold only with the agreement of existing owners, so owners keep control. A plc may sell shares to the public, raising big sums but risking takeover and has to publish more information. Ask: why might Zayn's Solar stay a Ltd? Answer: keeps control, avoids disclosure.

teach.heading: Public corporations
bullets: Owned by the government
Run for public benefit, not only profit
Funded by taxes and its own sales
Example: a fictional national railway corporation
teach.note: A public corporation is owned by the state and run by appointed managers; objectives are often public service. Avoid stating that a specific current organisation is or is not one unless sure; use the fictional Nile Valley Railways Corporation as the model. Ask: why might a government keep a railway public? Draw out service to everyone, jobs and national importance.

teach.heading: Worked example: dividends
teach.note: Take pupils through the dividend per share method. Ask what happens to dividend per share if profit distributed doubles. Check they can find the percentage owned: Zainab holds 2,000 of 10,000 shares = 20 per cent.

model.problem: Zayn's Solar Ltd has 10,000 shares. It pays 15,000 pounds in total dividends. Zainab owns 2,000 shares. How much does she receive?
steps: Dividend per share = 15,000 divided by 10,000 = 1.50 pounds
Check: she owns 20 per cent and 20 per cent of 15,000 is 3,000

teach.heading: Check: which form?
teach.note: Answer C. A is wrong because public limited companies sell shares to the public; B because limited liability protects personal assets; D because a sole trader cannot sell shares.

check.q: A business wants to raise 5 million pounds by selling shares on the stock exchange. Which form must it be?
check.why: Only a plc can sell shares to the public on a stock exchange.

teach.heading: Choosing the right form
bullets: Small, low risk, one owner: sole trader
Two professionals: partnership
Wants protection from debt: limited company
Large, needs big capital: plc
teach.note: Run a decision tree activity. Pupils decide for three scenarios. Evaluate: limited liability protects owners but a company has more legal paperwork. In the exam, use evidence from the given business.

practice: Eight friends each invest 5,000 pounds in a Ltd. It collapses owing 200,000 pounds. What is the most each friend can lose?
State two differences between a Ltd and a plc.
Explain one reason a government might run a business as a public corporation.
independent: Core: Match six features (for example 'owned by the state', 'shares sold on the stock exchange') to the correct form.
Extend: Explain two advantages of limited liability for the owner of Zayn's Solar.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): 'Becoming a plc is always the best way for a successful Ltd to grow.' Use pros, cons and a judgement.
exit: Define limited liability in one sentence.
Name the form of business owned by the government.
Big question answer: why would an owner want protection from business debts?
lessons.homework: Choose a business you know and decide whether it is more likely a sole trader, Ltd or plc; give two reasons.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a flowchart for choosing the form. EAL: create a glossary for shares, dividend, liability. Stretch: investigate the reasons a family firm might refuse to float.

lessons.title: Stakeholders, franchises, social enterprises and multinationals
lessons.bigQuestion: Who else cares whether a business succeeds, apart from the owner?
objectives: Identify stakeholders and shareholders and their interests
Describe franchises, social enterprises and multinationals
Judge which ownership form suits a business
successCriteria: All: name three stakeholders and what each wants
Most: describe a franchise and a social enterprise
Some: justify a franchise or social enterprise for a given situation
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: multinationals and host countries
lessons.smsc: Social: community responsibility; Moral: fair dealing with all stakeholders

keywords.def: any person or group affected by or interested in a business
an owner of shares in a company
a business using another firm's brand and system in return for fees
the owner of the brand who sells the franchise
the person who buys and runs the franchise
a business run to achieve a social aim, with profits mainly reinvested
a business operating in more than one country

starter: Name the form of business that can sell shares to the public.
Define limited liability.
State one advantage of being a sole trader.

teach.heading: Stakeholders
bullets: Owners and shareholders: profit and dividends
Employees: pay, security and good conditions
Customers: quality and fair prices
Suppliers: prompt payment
Community and government: jobs, tax and safety
teach.note: Use the fictional Al-Noor Bakery Ltd. Ask pupils to say what each group wants and where interests clash: higher wages for workers versus higher dividends for shareholders. Stress that a shareholder is a type of stakeholder but not every stakeholder is a shareholder. Link to ethics: treating customers, workers and suppliers fairly and honestly is something Islamic teaching emphasises; the teacher may expand with the class's own knowledge.

teach.heading: Franchises
bullets: Franchisee pays a fee and a share of sales
Uses the franchisor's brand, products and training
Lower risk because the idea is proven
Less freedom and profit shared with the franchisor
teach.note: Use the fictional Burger Barn franchise. Franchisee pays 20,000 pounds to start and 5 per cent of sales. Ask: who benefits? The franchisor expands with less capital; the franchisee gets a known brand. Drawbacks: rules on menu and prices, fees reduce profit. Misconception: a franchisee is not an employee; they own and run their own business.

teach.heading: Worked example: franchise fees
teach.note: Model the calculation, then ask whether the franchise is worthwhile. Link to risk and the proven brand. Many pupils forget to subtract fees from profit.

model.problem: Layla runs a Burger Barn franchise. Annual sales are 240,000 pounds. She pays 5% of sales to the franchisor. Her other costs are 190,000 pounds. Calculate her profit.

teach.heading: Social enterprises and multinationals
teach.note: Contrast. A social enterprise is a business with a social purpose: for example the fictional Bright Start Cafe trains young unemployed people and reinvests profit. It still has to cover its costs. A multinational has operations in several countries: the fictional Orion Foods has factories in four countries. Benefits to the firm: new markets, cheaper labour; drawbacks: complex management. Detailed host-country effects come in Unit 1.5.

right.title: Multinational
points: Gains new markets and lower costs

teach.heading: Check: stakeholder or franchise?
teach.note: Answer C. Distractor A confuses a franchisor with a franchisee; B confuses with a shareholder.

check.q: Which statement about a franchisee is correct?
options: Owns the brand and sells licences
Is an employee of the franchisor
Pays fees to use a brand and runs the outlet
check.why: A franchisee runs the outlet using the franchisor's brand in return for fees.

teach.heading: Which ownership form fits?
bullets: Wants proven brand: franchise
Wants to help the community: social enterprise
Wants world markets: multinational
Match the choice to the owner's aims
teach.note: Use a quick-fire scenario set so pupils practise justification. For each ask for one benefit and one drawback. Remind them that in the exam, a recommendation needs a reason linked to the context.

practice: List three stakeholders of a school uniform shop and what each wants.
Burger Barn charges 6% of sales. A franchisee has sales of 150,000 pounds. Calculate the fee.
Describe one difference between a franchise and a social enterprise.
independent: Core: Complete a stakeholder grid for Al-Noor Bakery Ltd with two interests per group.
Extend: Explain how the interests of employees and shareholders may conflict.
Stretch: Justify (6 marks): Khalid has 30,000 pounds and wants to open a cafe. Should he start his own brand or buy a franchise costing 20,000 pounds plus 5% of sales?
exit: Define franchise.
Give one benefit of franchising to the franchisor.
Big question: name one stakeholder who is not the owner and what they want.
lessons.homework: Research a franchise business near you and note who the franchisor and franchisee are.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a stakeholder sorting grid. EAL: show examples of well-known franchises. Stretch: analyse why a social enterprise might struggle to grow.

lessons.title: Market research: finding out before you spend

successCriteria: All: define primary and secondary research and name two methods of each
Most: choose a suitable method for a given business and say why

keywords.def: collecting and analysing information about customers and the market
new information collected first-hand for a specific purpose
existing information collected by someone else
descriptive opinions and feelings
numerical data that can be counted
selling a product in a small area first to gauge reaction

starter: Name two location factors.
Define e-commerce.
Why might a business choose a cheaper location even if it is further from customers?

teach.heading: Why research?
bullets: Finds customer needs and gaps in the market
Reduces the risk of failure
Helps set price, product and promotion
Checks reactions to a new idea
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Layla's Lunchbox, a healthy school-meal start-up. She plans to spend 15,000 pounds; asking 200 parents first could save that if nobody wants it. Ask: what could go wrong if she only asks friends? Introduce risk. Ensure pupils see research reduces risk but does not remove it.

teach.heading: Primary research methods
bullets: Surveys and questionnaires
Focus groups: a small group discusses the product
Observation: watching how customers behave
Test marketing: a trial in a small area
teach.note: Match each with Layla's. Questionnaire: 150 parents asked about price. Focus group: eight parents taste samples. Observation: counting how many pupils buy the snacks at the tuck shop. Test marketing: sells at one school for a month. Discuss benefit: relevant and up to date; limitation: expensive and slow.

teach.heading: Secondary research and types of data
teach.note: Compare. Secondary sources: internet, market reports, government reports. Cheaper and fast but may be out of date or not specific. Then link qualitative (a parent says the meals look dull) and quantitative (62 per cent would pay 3 pounds). Ask which data is easier to chart. Note social media can provide both, but opinions on it may not represent all customers.

right.title: Secondary research
points: May be out of date or general

teach.heading: Worked example: reading survey results
teach.note: Model the percentage and the judgement of reliability. Ask whether 40 parents at one school gate is a good sample. Draw out sample size and bias: only one area. Remind pupils that percentages should be calculated from the sample total.

model.problem: Layla surveys 250 parents. 175 say they would buy her lunchbox at 3 pounds. What percentage would buy, and how reliable is it?
steps: Check the sample: 250 parents is reasonably large
But if all came from one school the result may be biased
model.answer: 70% would buy; reliable only if the sample is varied

teach.heading: Check: method
teach.note: Answer C. Question gives a group discussing opinions - focus group. Distractor B is a trial sale.

check.q: Eight parents try Layla's meals and discuss them with a researcher. Which method is this?
check.why: A small group discussing a product with a facilitator is a focus group.

teach.heading: Reliability and social media
bullets: Large, random samples are more reliable
Biased questions give biased answers
Old data may no longer be true
Social media comments are opinions of those who post
teach.note: Ask pupils to spot the bias in 'Don't you agree our delicious meals are great value?' Discuss leading questions. Discuss honesty: Islamic ethics emphasise truthfulness, so a business should report results honestly even if they disappoint. Say that the teacher may expand with class discussion.

practice: Layla's survey: 90 of 120 parents like the idea. Calculate the percentage.
State two advantages of secondary research.
Explain one limitation of a focus group.
independent: Core: Design five questions for a questionnaire for a fictional school uniform shop, including one quantitative and one qualitative.
Extend: Explain why test marketing is useful before a national launch.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Layla can spend 800 pounds on a survey or use free government reports. Which should she use? Give a judgement.
exit: Define primary research.
Give one qualitative and one quantitative example.
Big question: one way to find out what customers want without guessing.

lessons.send: SEND: provide sentence starters for survey questions. EAL: use pictures for focus group and observation. Stretch: discuss sample bias with examples.

keywords.def: identifying and meeting customer needs profitably
a group of customers with similar characteristics
a small, specialised part of a market
a very large market with many customers

starter: Name one primary research method.
What is a qualitative result?
Why does a business do market research?

teach.heading: What marketing does
bullets: Identifies customer needs
Meets them with the right product
Builds relationships and loyalty
Responds to changing tastes and spending
teach.note: Bismillah. Use the fictional Tahir's Trainers. Ask: what does marketing mean? Pupils often say adverts; stress it covers research, product, price, place and promotion. Loyalty: a customer who returns costs less than winning a new one. Link to changes: a fall in incomes may mean customers want cheaper shoes, and competition may force a response.

teach.heading: Market orientation and product orientation
teach.note: Show the difference. A market-orientated firm researches first. A product-orientated firm invents then sells. Ask which is riskier. Product orientation can work with a new invention, but only if people want it. Misconception: market orientation does not mean copying competitors; it means responding to customers.

right.title: Product orientation
points: Based on the firm's own idea
Higher risk if nobody wants it

teach.heading: Segmentation
bullets: Location: city, town, region
Demographics: gender, family, occupation
Lifestyle: sporty, quiet, adventurous
Income: budget or luxury
Age: teenagers, adults, over 60s
teach.note: Take Tahir's Trainers and design a plan for each segment. Teenagers who want fashion; over 60s who want comfort; low-income families who need cheap. Ask why segmentation helps: messages, prices and products fit each group. Note the exam may give data by segment and ask which to target.

teach.heading: Niche and mass marketing
teach.note: Table. Niche: small market, higher prices possible, less competition, but limited sales. Mass: many customers, lower prices, economies of scale, but big competitors. Ask which suits a small firm. Ask which would suit a multinational. Evaluate with context.

teach.heading: Worked example: share change
teach.note: Show percentage change as 'change over original'. Note the common error of dividing by the new figure. Then ask whether the firm should be pleased and what else they would want to know (market growth).

model.problem: Tahir's sales rose from 80,000 pounds to 92,000 pounds. The market total stayed at 800,000. Calculate the percentage change in sales and the new market share.

teach.heading: Check: segment
teach.note: Answer B. A is location; C is age; D is income.

check.q: A gym offers evening classes for people who like outdoor sports and healthy eating. Which segmentation is this?
check.why: Interest in outdoor sport and healthy eating describes lifestyle.

practice: Tahir's sales were 50,000 pounds in a market worth 500,000. Calculate market share.
Give three ways to segment the market for a bicycle shop.
Explain one benefit of a niche market.
independent: Core: Segment the market for a fictional cafe by age and income and say what to offer each group.
Extend: Explain why a market-orientated business is less likely to fail.

exit: Define niche market.

lessons.title: The marketing mix: product, life cycle and the Boston matrix
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do some products last for decades while others vanish within a year?
objectives: Describe the product element of the mix: new product development, goods and services, packaging

successCriteria: All: name the four Ps and the stages of the life cycle

Some: recommend extension strategies for a product in decline

keywords.def: the combination of product, price, place and promotion
the stages a product passes through from launch to decline
action to lengthen a product's life
a tool that classifies products by market share and market growth
high market share in a fast-growing market
high market share in a slow-growing market

starter: Define market segmentation.
Name one niche market.
What is market orientation?

teach.heading: The four Ps and the product
bullets: Product, price, place, promotion
Product: goods or services, design, packaging
New product development: idea, research, testing, launch
Packaging protects, informs and attracts
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Sunrise Juices. Ask pupils to list the four Ps. Then go deep on product: a good must be safe and as described. Packaging must be honest; Islamic ethics value honesty in trade, and the teacher can expand without quoting. New product development: idea, market research, prototype, testing, launch. Many ideas fail: ask why testing saves money.

teach.heading: The product life cycle
teach.note: Use the cycle. Stages: development (cost, no sales), introduction (low sales), growth (rising), maturity (sales peak and level), decline (falling). Ask pupils to place Sunrise's Mango Boost. Extension strategies: new flavours, new packaging, new markets, price cuts, advertising. Misconception: every product reaches decline at a different speed; fashion fast, salt slow.

teach.heading: Extension strategies
bullets: New packaging or design
New flavour or version
Sell in a new market or country
Fresh advertising or a promotion
teach.note: Give Mango Boost, in maturity, sales stuck at 40,000 bottles a month. Ask pupils to choose two strategies and say what each costs. Draw out that extension can reverse falling sales, but costs money and may not work.

teach.heading: Boston matrix
teach.note: Explain axes: market share across, market growth up. Stars need investment, cash cows fund others, problem children could become stars or dogs, dogs may be dropped. Misconception: a dog is not always loss-making, but its prospects are poor. Ask pupils to classify Sunrise's four products with the table.

teach.heading: Check: life cycle
teach.note: Answer A. Sales rising quickly with rising profit is growth. Maturity is level sales.

check.q: Sunrise's Green Detox drink has sales rising fast and new retailers stocking it. Which stage is this?
check.why: Quickly rising sales as more retailers stock the product is the growth stage.

teach.heading: Worked example: using the matrix
teach.note: Model a decision from numbers. Ask: what would you do with a dog? Answer options: drop, or reposition. Remind that the matrix is a snapshot and needs updating.

model.problem: Sunrise's Plain Apple has 3% market share in a market growing 1% a year, and costs 12,000 pounds to make. What should the firm consider?
steps: Low share and low growth: this is a dog
Option: stop selling and use the money elsewhere
Option: check whether it helps the sales of other products before dropping
model.answer: Likely to drop it, unless it supports other sales

practice: Place a product with falling sales and fewer shops stocking it in the life cycle.
Give two extension strategies for a snack in maturity.
Explain what a business should do with a star product.
independent: Core: Draw a life cycle graph and label each stage for a fictional phone.
Extend: Explain how packaging can add value to a product.
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): A firm with one cash cow, two stars and two dogs has 100,000 pounds to invest. How should it allocate it?
exit: Name the stages of the life cycle.
What is a cash cow?

Choose a pricing strategy for a given situation

Some: justify a pricing strategy using evidence

keywords.def: adding a fixed percentage or amount to unit cost
a low launch price to win customers
a high launch price for a new, desirable product
setting price in line with rivals
temporary price cuts such as sales and offers
the cost of making one item

starter: Name the four Ps.
What is a niche market?
Name the five stages of the life cycle.

teach.heading: Why price matters
bullets: Price affects sales, profit and image
Too high loses customers
Too low may not cover costs
Must fit target customers
teach.note: Bismillah. Use fictional Zahra's Bags. If the bag costs 18 pounds to make and sells for 15, the business loses. Ask pupils what else price signals: quality. Fairness: a business that raises prices unfairly because customers have no other choice can damage trust; teachers can expand on ethics in trade without quoting.

teach.heading: Five strategies
bullets: Cost-plus: unit cost plus a markup
Penetration: low price to enter the market
Skimming: high price for a new, exciting product
Competitive: match rivals' prices
Promotional: short-term offers
teach.note: Give each a quick scenario. Zahra's: cost-plus to ensure profit. A new smartwatch uses skimming to earn from early adopters. A cafe next to rivals uses competitive pricing. A launch sale uses promotional pricing. Penetration requires being able to bear lower profit early; risk of customers leaving when price rises.

teach.heading: Worked example: cost-plus
teach.note: Ask pupils to add markup to cost. Check that 40 per cent markup is of cost, not of selling price. Extend: profit per bag = 7.20; for 500 bags sold profit 3,600.

model.problem: A bag costs 18 pounds to make. Zahra adds a 40% markup. Find the selling price, and the profit on 500 bags.

teach.heading: Choosing a strategy
teach.note: Use table to link strategy to situation. Pupils practise matching. Drive the point that the best strategy depends on the market, product and aims. Skimming is risky if copied quickly.

head: Strategy
Best when
Risk
rows: Low profit, hard to raise price

teach.heading: Check: strategy
teach.note: Answer B. Setting a low launch price to win customers quickly is penetration.

check.q: A new streaming app sets a very low price in its first three months to gain subscribers. Which strategy is this?
check.why: A low price to enter a market and win customers fast is penetration pricing. Promotional pricing is also temporary, but its aim is short-term sales on established products.

teach.heading: Evaluating price decisions
bullets: Look at costs, competitors and customers
Consider the product's life cycle stage
Think about the image the price creates
Judge short-term versus long-term effect
teach.note: Tell pupils that in evaluation questions, they should weigh up at least two factors and make a decision. Give an example: Zahra's has 30 rivals selling at 22 pounds. Cost-plus at 25.20 might lose customers; competitive pricing may reduce profit but keep sales.

practice: A cake costs 6 pounds. Add a 50% markup. What is the price?
Explain one risk of penetration pricing.
State two reasons a business might use promotional pricing.

Big question: how low before it stops paying?

References from past employers
teach.note: Show a short job description and person specification for a shop assistant. Pupils decide which statement belongs in each. Misconception: the two are often confused: one describes the job, the other describes the person.

teach.heading: The process
teach.note: Use cycle. At shortlisting, the firm compares each application to the person specification. At interview it asks questions and may add tests. Honesty: applicants should be honest on CVs, and employers honest about the job, which links to trust and truthfulness in dealing.
cycle: Write job description and person specification

teach.heading: Internal and external recruitment
teach.note: Compare. Internal: cheaper, quicker, motivates staff, who know the firm, but a smaller choice and creates a gap elsewhere. External: new ideas and bigger choice, but costly and slower, and new staff need induction. Ask pupils which they would choose for a manager role.

teach.heading: Legal controls
bullets: Equal opportunities: no unfair discrimination
Minimum wage: lowest legal hourly rate
Firms must follow the law in every country they operate in
Breaking the law risks fines and a poor reputation
teach.note: Keep it factual: do not quote specific current wage figures unless given in a question. Use fictional numbers. Equal opportunities: choose by skills, not by unrelated personal characteristics. Fair treatment of workers is also a theme in Islamic ethics; the teacher may expand and invite pupils to discuss.

teach.heading: Check: document
teach.note: Answer B. The person specification describes the person; the job description describes the duties.

check.q: Which document lists the skills and qualities a successful applicant should have?
check.why: The person specification describes the ideal person. The job description lists duties; confusing the two is the usual error.

teach.heading: Worked example: cost of a recruitment
teach.note: Model the calculation and then the evaluation: cheaper does not always mean better. Ask what else matters: skills and fit with the specification.

model.problem: Seaside Ice Cream pays 450 pounds to advertise a post externally. Internal recruitment would cost 100 pounds of manager time. The new employee will be paid 9 pounds an hour for 30 hours a week. Find the extra cost of external recruitment and the weekly wage.
steps: Compare: the extra cost equals more than one week's wage
model.answer: 350 pounds extra; wage 270 pounds a week

practice: Seaside needs 6 seasonal staff for 12 weeks at 8 pounds an hour for 20 hours a week. Calculate the total wage bill.
State one benefit and one drawback of internal recruitment.
Explain why a person specification helps with shortlisting.
independent: Core: Write a job description and a person specification for a fictional shop assistant.
Extend: Explain two reasons why Seaside Ice Cream might use seasonal staff.

Stretch: Justify (6 marks): A cafe needs a new manager. Should it promote its supervisor or recruit externally? Use the information that the supervisor has two years' experience and the cafe needs new ideas.
exit: Define equal opportunities.
Name two types of employment.
Big question: what makes the right person for the job?
lessons.homework: Find a real job advert and identify one duty and one skill required.
lessons.send: SEND: provide labelled examples of job description and person specification. EAL: pre-teach vacancy, shortlist. Stretch: investigate why job sharing might help some workers.

lessons.title: Market research: evidence, secondary sources and social media
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a business trust the information it uses to make a big decision?
objectives: Explain how market research reduces risk and gives evidence for decisions
Describe online sources, market reports and government reports as secondary research
Explain the role of social media in gathering data and why data must be dependable
successCriteria: All: state how research reduces risk and name three secondary sources
Most: judge one source for cost, age and relevance
Some: evaluate whether data from a social media poll is dependable enough for a 24,000 pound decision
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and sample size; ICT: judging online sources
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty (sidq) when collecting and reporting what customers say

keywords.def: facts and data that support a decision
the chance that a decision turns out badly
using information that already exists, collected by someone else
a published study of an industry, often written by a research firm and sold for a fee
official statistics and studies published by public bodies, often free
data that is accurate, up to date, unbiased and relevant to the question

starter: Define primary research and give two methods.
Give one qualitative and one quantitative example of data about a cafe.
Why might a start-up choose a focus group rather than a large survey?

teach.heading: Research reduces risk
bullets: Every big decision has a risk of failure
Research gives evidence, not guesses
Evidence shows demand before money is spent
It reduces risk but never removes it
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Hana's Halal Bakehouse wants to open a second branch costing 24,000 pounds. Ask: what could she do before signing the lease? Draw out that research tells her how many people might buy, what they will pay and who the competitors are. Stress the word 'reduces'. A decision backed by evidence is easier to defend to a bank or a partner, and easier to review later if it goes wrong.

teach.heading: Secondary sources
teach.note: Go through the table. Hana has not collected any of this herself, so it is secondary. Ask which is cheapest (government reports, often free) and which is most specific (market report, but it can cost hundreds or thousands of pounds - say 'a fee', no exact figure needed). Emphasise date: check when it was published. Competitor websites and review sites count as online sources, but anyone can post anything online, so check who wrote it.

head: Source
Example for Hana
Strength
Weakness
rows: Competitor menus, review sites, news articles
Report on the UK bakery industry
Can be expensive; may not fit her town
General; may be out of date

teach.heading: Social media as a data source
bullets: Polls and comments show opinions quickly and cheaply
Reviews and shares show what customers like
Can spot trends and complaints early
Only those who post are heard
teach.note: Hana posts a poll on her page and reads the comments under rivals' posts. Link to primary and secondary: her own poll is primary research; reading rivals' comments is closer to secondary. Be clear that a social media poll is quick but the people who respond are self-selected: usually existing followers, often younger, often the most enthusiastic. Ask: who is missing from her results?

teach.heading: Worked example: is the data dependable?
teach.note: Model the calculation then the judgement. Dependable data needs four tests: accurate, up to date, unbiased, relevant. Pupils often stop at the percentage; push them to say whether it can be trusted. Link to honesty: reporting a poor result truthfully protects the business from a costly mistake.

model.problem: Hana's poll gets 400 votes. 312 vote yes to opening a second branch. Her followers are mostly aged 18-25. Should she rely on the result?
steps: Percentage yes = 312 divided by 400 = 0.78, so 78 per cent
Is the sample large? 400 is reasonable
Is it representative? Followers are mostly 18-25 and already like her bakery
Is it unbiased? Only people who chose to vote took part
model.answer: 78 per cent yes, but not fully dependable: the sample is self-selected and narrow. Combine it with a survey of local residents and government population data.

teach.heading: Check: secondary or primary?
teach.note: Answer B. Government population statistics already exist and were collected by someone else. A is her own poll (primary), C is first-hand observation (primary), D is a focus group (primary). Watch for pupils who think 'online' means secondary: her own social media poll is online but primary.

check.q: Which of these is secondary research for Hana?
options: A poll she posts on her own page
Government statistics on how many families live in the area
Counting customers who enter a rival bakery
Eight neighbours tasting new cakes and giving views
check.why: Government statistics already exist and were collected by someone else. The others are collected first-hand, so they are primary.

teach.heading: Why data must be dependable
bullets: Wrong data leads to wrong decisions
Check the date, the author and the sample
Leading questions bias answers
Combine several sources to cross-check
teach.note: Misconception to tackle: 'more data always means better data'. Ten thousand biased answers are still biased. Give a leading question: 'Wouldn't you agree our cakes are the best in town?' Ask pupils to rewrite it neutrally. Islamic ethos: honesty in business is a core value; a business should not twist results to get the answer it wants. Do not attribute any specific text; keep it as a principle.

practice: Calculate the percentage: 156 of 600 followers vote yes in a poll.
State two advantages and one disadvantage of using government reports.
Hana finds a market report that is four years old. Explain one reason it may not be dependable.
independent: Core: Copy and complete a table of three secondary sources for a halal grocery shop: example, one strength, one weakness.
Extend: Explain how social media could help Hana find out what customers think of a rival, and one limit of this data (4 marks).

Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): Hana can pay a firm for a market report or rely on a free social media poll and government statistics. Which should she use before spending 24,000 pounds? Justify your judgement.
exit: State one way market research reduces risk.
Name two secondary sources.
Big question: give one reason data might not be dependable.
lessons.homework: Find one online article about a local business and write three lines on whether it is dependable: author, date, bias.
lessons.send: SEND: give the table pre-filled with gaps; sentence starter 'This data is not dependable because...'. EAL: pair the terms with pictures of a report and a phone. Stretch: assess how self-selection affects a poll.

lessons.title: Market share and responding to a changing market
lessons.bigQuestion: If a business sells more than last year, can it still be losing ground?
objectives: Calculate and interpret market share
Analyse market share to compare businesses and track performance
Explain how a business can respond to shifting needs, spending patterns and increased competition
successCriteria: All: calculate market share using the formula
Most: explain why share can fall when sales rise
Some: recommend and justify a response to a new competitor
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages and percentage change
lessons.smsc: Social: fair competition and treating rivals with respect

keywords.def: a business's sales as a percentage of total sales in the market
the total sales of all businesses in a market
an increase in the total sales of the market
another business selling similar products to the same customers
how customers choose to spend their money, for example more on value and less on luxuries

starter: Name two ways to segment a market.
What is the difference between a niche and a mass market?
Give one reason why customers' needs might change.

teach.heading: What is market share?
bullets: Share of the whole market that one business wins
Measured by sales revenue or number of units
Market share (%) = firm's sales / total market sales x 100
A larger share usually means a stronger position
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Zaytun Coffee Stop, one of several coffee shops in a town. Write the formula and read it as 'my slice of the pie'. The total market is every business's sales added together, including ours. Point out the answer is always a percentage between 0 and 100, and all shares in a market add up to 100 per cent.

teach.heading: Worked example: calculate market share
teach.note: Model slowly; insist on the same units (both in pounds, same year). Then do the second step: change in share. Ask why 15 per cent is only meaningful when compared with rivals or with earlier years.

model.problem: Zaytun Coffee Stop's sales are 360,000 pounds a year. Total sales of coffee shops in the town are 2,400,000 pounds. Calculate its market share.
steps: Formula: market share = firm's sales / total market sales x 100

teach.heading: Can sales rise but share fall?
teach.note: This is the key insight. Zaytun's sales rose from 300,000 to 330,000, up 10 per cent. But the whole market grew faster, from 2,000,000 to 2,500,000, up 25 per cent. Old share: 300,000 / 2,000,000 = 15 per cent. New share: 330,000 / 2,500,000 = 13.2 per cent. Competitors grew faster than Zaytun. Ask: should the owner celebrate? Discuss what to do next.

teach.heading: Check: reading market share
teach.note: Answer C. Share = 90,000 / 600,000 x 100 = 15 per cent. Distractor A is sales divided by 100 and D is 90,000 divided by 690,000 (adding to the total wrongly). Remind pupils that the market total already includes the firm.

check.q: A bakery sells 90,000 pounds a year. The whole market sells 600,000 pounds. What is its market share?
check.why: 90,000 / 600,000 x 100 = 15 per cent. 6.7 comes from dividing the wrong way round (600,000 / 90,000).

teach.heading: Responding to change
bullets: Shifting needs: adapt the product range
Spending patterns: offer value or lower-price options
Increased competition: differentiate, improve service, promote
Keep checking research and market share
teach.note: Use three mini-cases for Zaytun. 1) Needs shift: more customers want sugar-free drinks, so add sugar-free syrups and food. 2) Spending falls when household costs rise: add a 'small and cheap' range, loyalty stamps, meal deals. 3) A national chain opens nearby: stress what makes Zaytun different (friendly service, halal-friendly menu, local sourcing) and increase local promotion. Ask which response suits which change and what each costs.

teach.heading: Match the change to a response
teach.note: Pupils justify in pairs. There can be more than one sensible answer; marks go to a reason linked to the change. Reinforce that a business responds using evidence: market research and market share figures tell it when and what to change. Quote no external statistics.

head: Change in the market
Possible response
Why it helps
rows: Loyalty card, better service, local advertising
Improve quality or add value instead of copying

practice: Calculate market share: sales 48,000 pounds, market 320,000 pounds.
Last year a firm had 12 per cent share; this year it has 10 per cent while its sales rose. Give one possible reason.
Give one way a shop could respond if customers start spending less.
independent: Core: A halal takeaway has sales of 75,000 pounds in a market worth 500,000 pounds. Calculate its share, then calculate it again after sales rise to 84,000 pounds and the market to 700,000 pounds.
Extend: Explain why the owner should not judge success on sales alone (4 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a large chain opens next to a small family shop. Should the shop cut its prices or improve its service? Justify your recommendation.
exit: Write the market share formula.
Calculate: sales 20,000 pounds, market 250,000 pounds.
Big question: how can a business with rising sales still be losing ground?
lessons.homework: Choose a local shop. Describe two ways it could respond if a rival opened next door, and which you recommend.
lessons.send: SEND: provide the formula on a card and a calculator template. EAL: practise 'share' and 'market' with a pie-chart picture. Stretch: calculate percentage change in sales and market, then compare.

lessons.title: Packaging and why it matters
lessons.bigQuestion: How much of a product's success is in the box?
objectives: State the functions of packaging
Explain why packaging is important for sales, brand and customers
Weigh the cost and environmental impact of packaging decisions
successCriteria: All: list four functions of packaging
Most: explain how packaging helps a business sell a product
Some: evaluate whether to pay more for premium packaging
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: materials; Science: preservation; Maths: unit cost and percentages
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest labelling; avoiding waste as part of looking after resources entrusted to us

keywords.def: the container or wrapper around a product
stopping the product from being damaged or spoiled
information printed on the pack, such as ingredients and allergens
how customers see and feel about a brand
the cost of making one item

starter: Name the four Ps of the marketing mix.
Give one example of a product life cycle extension strategy.
What is a brand?

teach.heading: What does packaging do?
bullets: Protects the product in transport and storage
Keeps food fresh and hygienic
Gives information and legal labelling
Promotes the brand and attracts customers
teach.note: Bismillah. Hold up or describe two packs of dates: a plain plastic tub and a boxed gift set. Ask what each tells the customer. Packaging is part of the product element of the marketing mix. Functions: protect, preserve, inform, promote, make it convenient to carry, store or use. Mention that food labels must carry accurate ingredient and allergen information in many countries including the UK; on halal products, a recognised certification mark helps customers trust the claim. Honest labelling is also an ethical matter: customers rely on what we print.

teach.heading: Why is it important?
teach.note: Use the compare slide. Packaging is often the first thing a customer sees in a shop or in a delivery. For an online seller it also needs to survive posting. Ask pupils to choose which side matters most for a luxury chocolate brand and which for a budget rice brand. Draw out: the answer depends on the target segment and on price positioning.

left.title: Benefits to the business
points: Stands out against rivals on the shelf

right.title: Costs and drawbacks
points: Raises the cost of each unit
Too much waste harms the environment
Poor labelling can break the law

teach.heading: Worked example: packaging and cost
teach.note: Model the unit cost and the share of cost. Then ask: if the owner uses cost-plus pricing with a 50 per cent markup, what happens to the price? Price = 2.25 x 1.5 = 3.375, so about 3.38 pounds. A customer may or may not pay 38 pence more: this is where the evaluation lies. Link to target market: gift buyers may pay; everyday shoppers may not.

model.problem: A box of date biscuits costs 1.20 pounds ingredients, 0.35 pounds packaging and 0.45 pounds labour to make. Premium packaging would add 0.25 pounds. Find the unit cost now, the new unit cost, and packaging's share of the new cost.
model.answer: Unit cost rises from 2.00 to 2.25 pounds; packaging becomes about 26.7 per cent of cost. It is worth it only if customers will pay a higher price.

teach.heading: Check: purpose of packaging
teach.note: Answer B. Tamper-evident seals protect and reassure the customer: protection and safety. A is promotion, C is price, D is about distribution. Use the whiteboards and ask pupils to explain why the others are less accurate.

check.q: A juice company adds a seal that shows if the bottle has been opened. Which function of packaging is this mainly?
options: Protecting the product and reassuring customers
check.why: A tamper-evident seal protects the product and builds trust. The other options are different marketing mix decisions.

teach.heading: Packaging, the environment and ethics
bullets: Customers increasingly notice plastic and waste
Recyclable or refillable packs can improve image
Sustainable materials may cost more
Honest packs: no misleading claims or pictures
teach.note: Ask: what is the trade-off between a cheaper plastic wrapper and a recyclable paper pack? Connect to stakeholders: customers, local council, environmental groups. Islamic ethos: stewardship (amanah) of resources and avoiding wastefulness are widely discussed values, so many Muslim customers and owners care about over-packaging; present it as a value the business may hold, not as a ruling. Do not quote texts unless you can verify them.

practice: List four functions of packaging for a box of chocolates.
Calculate: ingredients 0.80 pounds, packaging 0.20 pounds, labour 0.50 pounds. Find unit cost and packaging's percentage of it.
Explain one way packaging could help a new brand compete with a well-known rival.
independent: Core: Design (describe in words) packaging for a halal-certified snack for school children: three features and what each is for.
Extend: Explain two reasons a business might change to environmentally friendly packaging (4 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a small online seller is deciding between cheap plain packaging and expensive branded packaging. Which should it choose? Consider cost, brand and customer.
exit: State three functions of packaging.
Give one cost of improving packaging.
Big question: give one way packaging can affect a product's success.
lessons.homework: Choose a product at home. Write down its packaging, three things the pack tells you, and one way it could be improved.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a picture-based pack to label with functions. EAL: pre-teach protect, preserve, label. Stretch: calculate the price change using a 50 per cent markup.

lessons.title: Types of employment and equal opportunities
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a business be fair to everyone who applies to work for it, and still meet its own needs?
objectives: Distinguish full-time, part-time, job share, casual, seasonal and temporary employment
Explain why a business might use each type
Explain the purpose of equal opportunities law and its effect on a business
successCriteria: All: define the six types of employment
Most: recommend a suitable type for a given business need
Some: evaluate the costs and benefits to a small business of following equal opportunities law
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE and citizenship: rights at work; Maths: weekly wage calculations
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: justice ('adl) and respect for every person's dignity in hiring

keywords.def: working the standard full week set by the employer
working fewer hours than a full-time employee
two people share the hours and duties of one full-time job
working only when needed, with no guaranteed hours
working during a busy time of year only
employed for a limited period, such as to cover absence
the principle that people are treated fairly in recruitment and at work whatever their personal characteristics
treating someone unfairly because of a personal characteristic

starter: Name two documents used in recruitment.
What is the difference between internal and external recruitment?
What does shortlisting mean?

teach.heading: Six types of employment
teach.note: Bismillah. Context: fictional Barakah Bakery Cafe, busy at weekends, busier before Eid and in the summer. Use the table. Ask pupils to give a fictional worker for each row. Note that exact weekly hours for full-time differ between businesses and countries, so say 'the standard week set by the employer'. Casual workers may have no guaranteed hours but the business should still treat them fairly and pay what is agreed.

head: Type
What it means
Example at Barakah Bakery
rows: Two people share one full-time job
Two parents split the manager's role
Called in when needed, no set hours
Only during a busy time of year
Extra staff for the weeks before Eid
Cover for a staff member on leave for six months

teach.heading: Choosing the right type
bullets: Match staff hours to demand
Part-time and casual staff give flexibility
Full-time staff give stability and skill
Seasonal and temporary staff avoid long-term cost
teach.note: Link to cost and risk. Using casual and seasonal staff means the business pays only when it is busy, but those staff may have less loyalty and need training quickly. Ask: why might a business not want to run only on casual staff? (Training costs, high turnover, lower skill and commitment.) Ask: who might prefer part-time or job share? (Parents, students, carers, older workers.)

teach.heading: Worked example: weekly wage cost
teach.note: Model the formula weekly wage = hours x hourly rate, then add up. Note this uses an invented hourly rate; do not suggest it is the legal minimum. Point out the saving from not paying a casual worker at quiet times, and that the total number of hours is what matters for a small firm's cash flow.

model.problem: Barakah Bakery pays 11 pounds an hour. Plan A: 1 full-time baker (40 hours) + 2 part-timers (20 hours each). Plan B: 1 full-time baker (40 hours) + 2 casual workers who work 12 hours each in a quiet week. Find the weekly wage cost of each plan.
steps: Plan A hours = 40 + 20 + 20 = 80; cost = 80 x 11 = 880 pounds
Plan B hours = 40 + 12 + 12 = 64; cost = 64 x 11 = 704 pounds
model.answer: Plan A costs 880 pounds, Plan B 704 pounds: casual staff save 176 pounds in a quiet week, but offer less certainty for workers.

teach.heading: Equal opportunities law
bullets: Law protects workers and applicants from unfair treatment
Protected areas: gender, race, disability, religion, sexual preference, age
Applies to hiring, pay, promotion and dismissal
Details of the law differ between countries
teach.note: Name the characteristics the specification lists: gender, race, disability, religion, sexual preference and age. In the UK this is covered by the Equality Act 2010 (verify wording before quoting); other countries have their own laws, so for the exam pupils need the idea and its effect on businesses. Teach this factually and respectfully: the law requires fair treatment at work, and our school ethos of justice and respect for people's dignity applies to all. Examples: a job advert asking for 'young men only' is unlawful discrimination; refusing to consider a disabled applicant who can do the job with reasonable adjustments is unlawful; refusing someone time for religious worship without good reason can cause problems. Keep the discussion on business practice, not personal beliefs.

teach.heading: Check: spotting discrimination
teach.note: Answer C. Rejecting a candidate because of age rather than ability is discrimination. A and B select on skills; D is a normal requirement linked to the job. If pupils choose D, discuss that requirements must be genuinely needed for the role.

check.q: Which action is most likely to break equal opportunities law?
options: Rejecting a candidate with no food hygiene certificate for a kitchen job
Choosing the applicant with the strongest interview score
Rejecting an applicant because they are 58 and 'too old to learn'
Asking all applicants to be available at weekends because the cafe is open then
check.why: Rejecting someone because of age rather than ability is discrimination. The other choices are linked to the job's genuine requirements.

teach.heading: Effects on a business
teach.note: Use the compare slide to debate. Ask pupils to decide whether benefits outweigh costs for a small business. Evaluation phrases: 'in the short run', 'in the long run', 'it depends on the size of the business'. Costs include training managers, adjusting premises or equipment for a disabled employee, and the time needed to follow fair procedures; benefits include access to a wider pool of talent, a good reputation, loyal staff and avoiding claims and fines.

right.title: Costs to the business
points: Risk of costly claims if breached

practice: Which type of employment suits a worker needed only for the two weeks before Eid? Give a reason.
Calculate: 3 part-time staff work 15 hours each at 10 pounds an hour. Weekly wage cost?
Explain one benefit to a business of following equal opportunities law.
independent: Core: Match six workers to the correct employment type and give a reason for each (matching table provided).
Extend: Explain two advantages and one disadvantage to a business of using seasonal staff (6 marks).
Stretch: Evaluate (8 marks): a small cafe owner says equal opportunities law is a burden. To what extent do you agree? Reach a conclusion.
exit: Define job share and casual employment.
Name three characteristics protected by equal opportunities law.
Big question: one way to be fair to applicants and still meet the business's needs.
lessons.homework: Write a short job advertisement for a part-time role at a halal grocery that is fair to all applicants and describes the job without discriminating.
lessons.send: SEND: use a card-sort for the six types. EAL: pre-teach 'discriminate', 'seasonal', 'temporary' with examples. Stretch: discuss reasonable adjustments with a real-world scenario.

keywords.def: growing links between economies through trade, travel and communication
a good or service bought from abroad
a good or service sold abroad
the firms that supply materials and parts

More trade, travel and communication
Firms buy, make and sell worldwide

Sells online to 20 countries
Fabric from Turkey, sewing in Leicester
teach.note: Discuss: which opportunities and threats does Modest Threads face?

misconception.right: Small firms sell online worldwide and face foreign competitors too

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is a THREAT of globalisation for a UK firm?

practice.q: Explain one opportunity globalisation gives Modest Threads. (3 marks)

options: growing links between the world's economies

exit.q: Back to our ponder: Look at the labels on three things in your house. How many countries are involved in your everyday life?

the country where a multinational sets up
a tax on imports
sending profits back home

hook.text: A global car maker opens a factory in a small town. Who wins, and could anyone lose?
hook.a: Jobs and income for the town and lower costs for the firm; but local firms may struggle and profits may go abroad.

starter.q: A plc can raise money by ...

starter.a: e.g. a well-known car maker or food chain (any real example).

teach.heading: Why become a multinational?
bullets: Closer to customers abroad
Lower costs (labour, land)
Avoid trade barriers (tariffs)
Spread risk across markets

teach.heading: Ethics
bullets: Fair wages and safe work
Paying fair tax where profits are made
Protecting the environment

check.q: Which is a DRAWBACK for a host country?
options: Profits sent back to the home country

practice.q: Explain one benefit for a business of becoming a multinational. (3 marks)
practice.a: Lower production costs, e.g. cheaper labour abroad, which raises profit margins or allows lower prices.
practice.model: Point: lower costs. Explain: wages and land may be cheaper in the host country. Develop: the firm can cut prices or raise profit.

practice.q: Locating inside a trade bloc avoids ...

independent.q: In the portal box: 'A multinational opening a factory is always good for the host country.' Evaluate this statement (6 marks). Use the pupil PDF case of a fictional factory in Morocco.
independent.a: Benefits (jobs, skills, tax) against drawbacks (profit repatriation, local firms, environment); a supported judgement ('it depends on ...').
independent.model: The teacher writes the first point: 'The factory creates 2,000 jobs, raising incomes and spending in the area, which helps local shops.'

independent.q: Extend: name two benefits to a multinational of spreading risk.
independent.a: A downturn in one country can be balanced by sales elsewhere.

independent.q: Stretch: how could a host government reduce the drawbacks?
independent.a: Laws on wages and pollution; tax rules; require local suppliers.

exit.q: A host country is ...
exit.a: where the multinational sets up

exit.q: Back to our ponder: A global car maker opens a factory in a small town. Who wins, and could anyone lose?
exit.a: Jobs and income for the town and lower costs for the firm; but local firms may struggle and profits may go abroad.

objectives: To understand how to convert prices between currencies using an exchange rate
successCriteria: All: convert pounds into another currency by multiplying
Most: convert another currency into pounds by dividing
Some: compare costs after an exchange-rate change
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: multiplying and dividing by decimals; proportion
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest pricing; 'Woe to those who give less than due' (Al-Mutaffifin 83:1)

keywords.def: the price of one currency in terms of another
the money used in a country
change an amount from one currency to another

hook.text: A hoodie costs £20 in London. How would a shop in New York know what to charge in dollars?
hook.a: Use the exchange rate: if £1 = $1.25, then £20 = $25.

starter.q: Name two currencies other than the pound.
starter.a: e.g. US dollar, euro, Saudi riyal.

teach.heading: The exchange rate
bullets: The price of one currency in another
£1 = $1.25 means one pound buys 1.25 dollars
Pounds to foreign: multiply
Foreign to pounds: divide
teach.note: Spec 1.5.3. Calculators allowed in 4BS1.

model.problem: £1 = €1.16. A UK firm sells a jacket for £50. What is the price in euros? A French supplier charges €580: what is that in pounds?

teach.heading: Practice table

check.q: £1 = $1.25. What is $250 in pounds?
check.why: 250 ÷ 1.25 = 200. Multiplying gives 312.50, the common error.

practice.q: £1 = €1.16. A UK café imports Italian coffee costing €464. Calculate the cost in pounds. (2 marks)

lessons.title: 1.5 Exchange rate changes: importers and exporters
lessons.bigQuestion: If the pound becomes stronger, is that good news or bad news for UK businesses?
objectives: To understand how a change in the exchange rate affects the prices, competitiveness and profits of importers and exporters
successCriteria: All: state what a stronger pound does to export prices
Most: calculate the effect of a rate change on an import cost
Some: analyse how a firm might respond
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentage change
lessons.smsc: Moral: honest trade whatever the market does

keywords.def: a rise in the value of a currency
a fall in the value of a currency
how attractive a firm's prices and products are compared with rivals
a business that buys from abroad

hook.text: If the pound becomes stronger, is that good news or bad news for UK businesses?
hook.a: It depends: importers pay less (good); exporters' prices rise abroad (bad). SPICED: Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer.

teach.heading: SPICED and WIDEC
teach.note: Spec 1.5.4.

model.problem: A UK firm sells a £20 hoodie in the USA. The rate rises from £1 = $1.25 to £1 = $1.50.
steps: Hoodies are less competitive in the USA

model.problem: A UK shop imports $6,000 of stock. The rate rises from $1.25 to $1.50.

teach.heading: How firms respond
bullets: Exporter: keep the dollar price, accept less profit
Or compete on quality, not price
Importer: lower prices or keep the extra margin

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Launch the Teams poll; share results; explain the right answer and the trap in the others.

check.q: The pound gets weaker. A UK exporter's products abroad become ...
check.why: WIDEC: weak pound, exports cheaper.

practice.q: The rate falls from £1 = €1.20 to £1 = €1.00. A UK importer buys €3,000 of goods. Calculate the change in cost in pounds. (3 marks)
A strong pound is good for ...

independent.q: Case (pupil PDF): Modest Threads exports to the USA and imports fabric from Turkey. The pound strengthens. In the portal box analyse the overall effect on its profit (6 marks).
independent.a: Exports dearer in dollars (sales may fall) but Turkish fabric cheaper (costs fall); net effect depends on the share of sales abroad against imported costs.
independent.model: The teacher writes the first chain: 'A stronger pound means each £50 abaya costs more dollars, so American customers may buy fewer ...'

independent.q: Extend: write out SPICED and WIDEC in full.
independent.a: Strong Pound Imports Cheaper Exports Dearer; Weak (pound) Imports Dearer Exports Cheaper.

independent.q: Stretch: why might a firm not change its foreign price when the rate moves?
independent.a: Rates move often; price changes confuse customers; it may absorb the change in its margin.

exit.q: SPICED stands for ...
exit.a: Strong Pound Imports Cheaper Exports Dearer
options: Strong Pound Imports Cheaper Exports Dearer
Sales Profit Income Cost Expense Debt

exit.q: Back to our ponder: If the pound becomes stronger, is that good news or bad news for UK businesses?
exit.a: It depends: importers pay less (good); exporters' prices rise abroad (bad). SPICED: Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer.
